client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely overwhelmed trying to juggle my nursing shifts and taking care of my kids while my partner is deployed. I barely have time to breathe, and I’m constantly worried I’m failing at both work and parenting. Honestly, I’m not sure if talking about it will really help because I don’t see how therapy can change my situation—it’s just too much to handle.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying an immense load right now, and it’s completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when balancing such demanding responsibilities. While therapy can’t change the external pressures, it can help us explore how you’re interpreting and responding to them—do you think shifting your perspective on what “failing” means might ease some of the weight?

client: I don't know... when I think about shifting my perspective, it just makes me feel worse because I know I'm not meeting my own standards. Like yesterday I forgot my daughter's soccer practice, and at work I almost gave the wrong medication dose because I was so tired. Those feel like real failures to me, not just in my head.
therapist: Those sound like really difficult moments, and I hear how much they reinforce your belief that you're falling short. Can we explore what you think a "successful" parent and nurse would look like in these situations—are those standards realistic given your current circumstances?

client: A successful parent would never forget important things like soccer practice, and a good nurse would never make medication mistakes no matter how tired they are. But I guess... when I say it out loud, it does sound a bit extreme. It's just hard to accept anything less when people's wellbeing is at stake.
therapist: It makes sense that you hold yourself to such high standards when caring for others is so important to you. I wonder if we could balance that care for others with some compassion for yourself—what would you say to a colleague who made a similar mistake under similar pressures?

client: I'd probably tell my coworker to go easy on themselves—that everyone makes mistakes sometimes, especially when they're stretched so thin. But when it comes to me... it's different somehow. Like I should be able to handle it all perfectly no matter what. It feels weak to admit I have limits.
therapist: You've spotted such an important difference between the kindness you'd show a colleague and the expectations you hold for yourself. What do you think it would feel like to extend that same understanding to yourself, even just a little?

client: It feels... scary, honestly. If I start cutting myself slack, what if I let important things slide? My kids and patients need me to be at my best. But at the same time, I'm so exhausted that this perfectionism thing clearly isn't working either. I'm stuck between feeling guilty if I try to be kinder to myself, and burned out if I don't.
therapist: That tension between self-compassion and responsibility is so real—it's like you're caught between fear of failing others and the reality of your own exhaustion. Could we explore what "being at your best" might look like if it included acknowledging your human limits?

client: I’ve never really thought about what “being at my best” would look like with limits—it’s always been about pushing through no matter what. But honestly, the idea of including limits makes me uncomfortable because it feels like I’m making excuses or lowering the bar. At the same time, I know I can’t keep going like this forever—it’s just hard to imagine finding a balance without feeling like I’m letting people down.
therapist: You're describing such an important dilemma—wanting to care for yourself while fearing it means compromising your care for others. What if we viewed acknowledging limits not as lowering the bar, but as setting a more sustainable one that actually allows you to show up consistently for those who need you?

client: That actually makes me tear up a little. I've never thought about it like that before—that taking care of myself could actually help me take better care of others in the long run. But it still feels selfish somehow... like I'm cheating my kids and patients out of what they deserve if I'm not giving every last ounce of energy I have.
therapist: It's moving to see this realization touch you so deeply—it shows how much you truly care. That "selfish" feeling makes complete sense when you've built your identity around giving so much to others—what would it be like to experiment with small acts of self-care and observe what happens to your ability to care for others?

client: I could try something small, like taking 10 minutes to sit with a coffee before my shift... but then I immediately think of all the things I could be doing instead—packing lunches, checking charts. It feels like those minutes would just add to my guilt pile. How do people do self-care without feeling like they're stealing time from others?
therapist: It's understandable that even small acts for yourself trigger thoughts about "stolen time"—that shows how deeply wired your caregiving mindset is. What if we viewed those 10 minutes as an investment that might actually make you more present when packing lunches or checking charts later?

client: I guess when you put it that way, it makes logical sense—like putting on your oxygen mask first. But in practice, I tried sitting for 5 minutes yesterday and just spent the whole time stressing about everything I wasn't doing. It feels like my brain won't let me relax even when I try. Maybe I'm just not built for this self-care stuff?
therapist: It sounds like even when you made space for yourself, your mind filled it with worries—that's actually very common when we first try to change long-held patterns. What do you think would happen if we treated those thoughts as background noise rather than urgent signals during your 5-minute breaks?

client: I don't know if I can just ignore those thoughts—they feel too important to dismiss as background noise. When I'm sitting there, my brain keeps screaming "You're wasting time!" and it feels so real and urgent. Maybe I need to work up to this more gradually, like starting with just 1 minute without beating myself up about it?
therapist: That sounds like a thoughtful approach—starting small and being gentle with yourself as you try something new. What if we viewed this 1-minute experiment as a chance to observe those "urgent" thoughts without letting them control your actions—what do you think you might notice?
